title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: WORD ORDER DOES THE ARTICLE'S WORK, and this is where M1's promise is paid. Russian has no a and no the, so the job moves into the order: what is already known goes first, and the NEW information goes last. Книга на столе is "the book is on the table" — we know the book, and where it is, is the news. На столе книга is "there is a book on the table" — we know the table, and the book is the news. Both are correct, and they are not interchangeable.

он, она and оно refer to things as well as people, and they follow the noun's GENDER rather than whether it is alive: a стол is он, a книга is она, молоко is оно. English has one "it" for all of them, so an English speaker reaches for оно and is wrong most of the time.

The joiners are the module's honest spend: и (and), но (but), а (and-but, marking a contrast between two things), тоже (also), потом (then, afterwards). а is the one with no clean English twin — it joins two halves that differ without contradicting, where но contradicts.

Keep the subject pronoun. Russian can drop я and in speech often does, especially in answers — but the past tense names a gender rather than a person, so был with no pronoun is genuinely ambiguous, and knowing when the drop sounds natural rather than clipped takes an ear you do not have yet. Write the pronoun; lose it later.

A turn is two or three short sentences, not one long one. Everything here is recombination: nearly every word came from M1–M9, and the work is holding a short exchange together rather than building a bigger sentence.

words.note: The third greeting, for the middle of the day — M2 had Здравствуйте for any hour and Доброе утро for the morning. добрый is the masculine shape of the same word that was доброе in front of утро: the greeting agrees with the time of day it names.

sentences.trap: The two words of the greeting have to agree, and they do so invisibly: доброе with the neuter утро, добрый with the masculine день. Getting them crossed is the commonest slip in Russian's politest phrase.
sentences.sound: DO-bry dyen' kak dye-LA. The ы of добрый is the hard back vowel, and день ends soft.

variations.cue: Good afternoon, Anna!
variations.changed: a name after a comma, as with every greeting in the course

variations.cue: Good morning! How are things?
variations.changed: the morning greeting instead — and its describing word changes with it

variations.cue: Hello! How are things with you?
variations.changed: the fuller, more careful version of both halves — the one to prefer with a stranger

mistake.why: день is masculine, so its describing word is добрый. доброе belongs with утро.

sentences.usage: Opening any conversation between about noon and the evening.
sentences.mnemonic: Доброе утро, добрый день. The greeting agrees with the part of the day it names.

words.note: The joiner English has no single word for. It links two halves that DIFFER without contradicting — "I'm fine, and you?", "this is a book, and that is a newspaper". Where но would set the halves against each other, а just turns the attention from one to the other. On its own with a pronoun it is the standard way of handing a question back.

sentences.trap: и, а and но all come out as "and" or "but" in English, and they are three different jobs: и adds, а turns, но contradicts. Choosing и here would sound as if you were listing yourself and the other person together.
sentences.sound: kha-ra-SHO spa-SEE-ba a vy. А is one unstressed vowel and leans onto вы.

variations.cue: Fine, thank you. And you, Anna?
variations.changed: the name added, which is warmer

variations.cue: Not good. And you?
variations.changed: M9's плохо as the answer — the handing-back half does not change

variations.display: Хорошо, спасибо. А как дела у вас?
variations.cue: Fine, thank you. And how are things with you?
variations.changed: the full question handed back instead of the two-word version

mistake.why: и adds one thing to another. Turning the question back on somebody is а вы?

sentences.usage: The second turn of every conversation you will have.
sentences.mnemonic: и adds, а turns, но contradicts. Three joiners, three jobs, one English word.

sentences.cue: I am a student and I work

words.note: "And", adding one thing to another. No comma in front of it when it simply joins two halves — Russian's comma rules are strict, and this is one of the places where the comma stays away.

sentences.trap: The second я is not optional at this level. Russian could drop it, and in speech often would — but the ending alone will not always name the person, and the habit is worth keeping until you can hear when to break it.
sentences.sound: ya stoo-DYENT ee ya ra-BO-ta-yoo. и is one short "ee", and it leans onto whatever follows it.

variations.cue: I am a student and I work (said by a woman)
variations.changed: студент → студентка: a different word, as it has been since M1

variations.display: Я работаю и я живу в Москве.
variations.cue: I work and I live in Moscow
variations.changed: two verbs joined instead of a noun and a verb

variations.display: Я студент, но я не работаю.
variations.cue: I am a student but I don't work
variations.changed: и → но, which contradicts rather than adds — and но takes a comma where и does not

mistake.why: No comma before и when it simply joins two halves. Russian's punctuation is stricter than English's in both directions.

sentences.usage: Saying two things about yourself in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: и joins and takes no comma. но contradicts and takes one.

sentences.display: Я хочу чай, но не хочу кофе.
sentences.cue: I want tea but I don't want coffee
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I want tea, but not want coffee"
sentences.literal: I want tea, but not want coffee

words.note: "But", setting one half against the other. It always takes a comma in front of it, where и takes none — that is the practical difference between them on the page.

sentences.trap: The second я really is dropped here, and that is allowed: when the person has not changed and the halves are joined, Russian leaves it out. This is the one place on the rung where the pronoun goes, and the rule elsewhere still holds.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chai no nye kha-CHOO KO-fye. но is short and flat, not the drawn-out English "but".

variations.display: Я хочу чай, но я не хочу кофе.
variations.cue: I want tea but I don't want coffee
variations.changed: the second я written out — equally correct, and a shade more deliberate

variations.cue: I want tea and coffee
variations.changed: и instead of но, so the halves add rather than contradict — and the comma goes

variations.display: Я хочу воду, но не хочу сок.
variations.cue: I want water but I don't want juice
variations.changed: swap the drinks — воду still bends, being feminine

mistake.display: Я хочу чай но не хочу кофе.
mistake.why: но takes a comma in front of it, always. It is the mirror of и, which takes none.

sentences.usage: Turning half an offer down — and the commonest use of но in ordinary speech.
sentences.mnemonic: Comma, но. No comma, и. The punctuation tells you which joiner you are looking at.

sentences.cue: Ivan is a student. Anna is a student too.

words.note: "Also", and it goes in front of what it adds — not at the end of the sentence, where English usually puts "too". Here it is in front of студентка, because it is the being-a-student that is shared.

sentences.trap: English puts "too" at the end and Russian puts тоже in front of the thing being shared, which means it also decides what the sentence claims: Анна тоже студентка says Anna is one as well, while Тоже Анна студентка would be pointing at another Anna.
sentences.sound: ee-VAN stoo-DYENT AN-na TO-zhe stoo-DYENT-ka. The ж of тоже is the s of "measure" again.

variations.cue: Ivan is a student. Anna too.
variations.changed: the second half cut to two words — тоже can stand alone as the whole reply

variations.cue: I am a student. Anna is a student too.
variations.changed: a pronoun in the first half instead of a name

variations.cue: Ivan works. Anna works too.
variations.changed: a shared verb rather than a shared noun — тоже still sits in front of it

mistake.why: тоже goes in front of what it adds, not at the end. Анна тоже студентка.

sentences.usage: Agreeing that somebody else is in the same position — a very common second half of a turn.
sentences.mnemonic: English adds "too" at the end. Russian puts тоже in front of the shared thing.

sentences.display: Сегодня я работаю. Потом я буду отдыхать.
sentences.cue: Today I am working. Afterwards I will rest.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "today I work. then I will-be rest-INFINITIVE"
sentences.literal: Today I work. Then I will-be to-rest

words.note: Today. Written with a г and said with a в — see-VOD-nya — one of the same small group of words as конечно, where the spelling and the sound part company. It joins вчера and завтра to complete the set.
"Then", in the sense of afterwards. It opens the second half of a turn and is the simplest way to put two events in order.

sentences.trap: Сегодня is said "see-VOD-nya" and there is no rule to derive it from — the г is pronounced as a в in a handful of very common words, and they have to be learned one at a time.
sentences.sound: see-VOD-nya ya ra-BO-ta-yoo pa-TOM ya BOO-doo ad-dy-KHAT'. The г of сегодня is a v.

variations.display: Сегодня я работаю. Потом я пойду домой.
variations.cue: Today I am working. Then I will go home.
variations.changed: a finished-event future in the second half, so no буду

variations.display: Вчера я купил хлеб. Потом я пошёл домой.
variations.cue: Yesterday I bought bread. Then I went home.
variations.changed: the whole turn moved into the past

variations.display: Завтра я буду работать. Потом я буду отдыхать.
variations.cue: Tomorrow I will work. Then I will rest.
variations.changed: the whole turn moved into the future

mistake.why: Two verbs cannot both carry an ending, and Сегодня я работаю is already about today. буду has no place here.

sentences.usage: Describing a day in two steps — the shortest real narrative in the course.
sentences.mnemonic: вчера, сегодня, завтра. Three words, three days, and the middle one is said with a v.

sentences.cue: Where is the key? It is on the table.

words.note: One row, four shapes, and the shape follows the noun's GENDER rather than whether it is alive: он for a masculine noun (ключ, стол, город), она for a feminine one (книга, газета), оно for a neuter one (молоко, письмо), они for more than one. English has a single "it" for every object, which is exactly why this needs its own row.

sentences.trap: English would say "it" here and an English speaker reaches for оно. But ключ is masculine, so the key is он. оно is only for neuter nouns, and there are far fewer of those than the English habit expects.
sentences.sound: gdye klyuch on na sta-LYE. Он is one short syllable with a clean o.

variations.cue: Where is the book? It is on the table.
variations.changed: книга is feminine, so the book is она

variations.cue: Where is the milk? It is in the shop.
variations.changed: молоко is neuter, so this is the one case where English's "it" and Russian's оно line up

variations.cue: Where is Ivan? He is at work.
variations.changed: the same он, this time about a person — Russian makes no distinction

mistake.why: ключ is masculine, so it is он. оно is only for neuter nouns like молоко and письмо.

sentences.usage: Answering a question about a thing without repeating its name.
sentences.mnemonic: The pronoun follows the noun's gender, not its aliveness. A table is he.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, do you speak Russian? A little.

words.note: "Excuse me" — the вы-form again, with the same polite -те as Здравствуйте and Дайте. It opens a question to a stranger and it also serves as a light apology; there is no separate word for the two jobs at this level.
"A little" — M6's много with не- fused onto the front, and it is written as one word. As an answer on its own it is the modest reply to any question about what you can do.

sentences.trap: Извините is a command in form — it is telling somebody to excuse you — but it is not heard as one. Its -те is what makes it polite, and leaving it off gives the ты-form this course does not write.
sentences.sound: eez-vee-NEE-tye vy ga-va-REE-tye pa-ROO-skee. Two words ending in the same polite -tye, one after the other.

variations.cue: Excuse me, do you speak Russian?
variations.changed: the question alone, without the answer attached

variations.cue: Excuse me, where is the shop?
variations.changed: the same opener in front of M7's question — this is what Извините is for

variations.cue: Sorry, I don't understand.
variations.changed: the apology sense, in front of M9's most useful sentence

mistake.why: Извини is the ты-form, and вы in the same breath contradicts it. With вы it is Извините.

sentences.usage: Stopping a stranger — and it is the first word of most useful conversations you will have.
sentences.mnemonic: The polite -те on Здравствуйте, Дайте and Извините is the same ending, doing the same job.

sentences.display: Сейчас я работаю, потом я пойду домой.
sentences.cue: Right now I am working, then I will go home
sentences.glossEn: lit. "now I work, then I will-go home-wards"
sentences.literal: Now I work, then I will-go homewards

words.note: "Now". It is what makes M4's one present tense unambiguous — Я работаю on its own is both "I work" and "I am working", and Сейчас я работаю can only be the second. In speech it is often cut down to "shchas".

sentences.trap: Both halves of the turn use a present-shaped verb and only one of them is a present tense. работаю is happening now; пойду looks the same and means "I will go", because it is a finished-event verb. M6's rule is doing the work here.
sentences.sound: see-CHAS ya ra-BO-ta-yoo pa-TOM ya pay-DOO da-MOY. Сейчас is stressed on the second syllable.

variations.display: Сейчас я работаю, потом я буду отдыхать.
variations.cue: Right now I am working, then I will rest
variations.changed: an everyday verb in the second half, so this future needs буду

variations.display: Сейчас я дома, потом я буду работать.
variations.cue: Right now I am at home, then I will work
variations.changed: no verb at all in the first half — the zero copula, on the last rung as on the first

variations.cue: Right now I am not working
variations.changed: one half only, with не in front of the verb

mistake.display: Сейчас я буду работаю, потом я пойду домой.
mistake.why: буду goes with a dictionary shape, never with a verb that already has an ending — and Сейчас is now, not later, so no future belongs in that half at all.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are doing and what comes next — a whole small plan in one turn.
sentences.mnemonic: Two present-looking verbs, two different times. Which is which depends on the verb, not the ending.

sentences.cue: Everything is fine, thank you. Goodbye!

words.note: "Everything", and the two dots matter: всё is everything, все is everybody. They are two different words, and the only thing telling them apart on the page is the ё — which is why this course always writes it, even though Russian print usually does not.

sentences.trap: всё and все are one letter apart and mean different things — one is a pile of things, the other is a crowd of people. In most Russian books both are printed все, and you are expected to work out which from the sentence. Write the dots.
sentences.sound: fsyo kha-ra-SHO spa-SEE-ba da svee-DA-nee-ya. Всё is one syllable, and the ё carries the stress as it always does.

variations.cue: Everything is fine
variations.changed: the first half alone — a complete answer to Как дела?

variations.cue: Everything is fine, thank you. And you?
variations.changed: the question handed back instead of the goodbye

variations.cue: Thank you, goodbye!
variations.changed: the closing half alone — how a shop conversation ends

mistake.why: Without the dots this is все, "everybody", and the sentence says something else. Everything is всё.

sentences.usage: Closing a conversation warmly — the last turn of the level, and the one you will use most.
sentences.mnemonic: всё is everything; все is everybody. Two dots are the whole difference.

comprehensionPool.cue: Good afternoon, Ivan! How are things?
Everything is fine, thank you. And you?
Where is the newspaper? It is on the table.
Excuse me, where is the shop?
I am a student and I work (said by a woman)

comprehensionPool.display: Сегодня я не работаю, потом я буду отдыхать.
comprehensionPool.cue: Today I am not working, then I will rest

comprehensionPool.display: Я хочу воду, но не хочу сок.
comprehensionPool.cue: I want water but I don't want juice
Where is the milk? It is in the shop.
Sorry, I don't understand. A little.
